newsitem.title: USA: El Paso condemnation pursuit bill now law.
newsitem.headline: El Paso condemnation pursuit bill now law.

text.p: El Paso Electric Co said Friday New Mexico's governor signed a bill which will allow the City of Las Cruces to seek condemnation of public use property belonging to El Paso Electric within its city limits. The new law takes effect immediately.
The utility pointed out the "ultimate result of the city's attempt to condemn and take over EPE's operations is still a long way from being determined."
Under New Mexico law, El Paso Electric is entitled to just compensation for its property in a condemnation.
Just compensation the difference between the value of the utility's entire system prior to the taking, as compared to the value of the entire system after the taking, El Paso said.
It noted a condemnation proceeding would determine the amount of just compensation.
But before Las Cruces can condemn the utility property, it said, the recovery of stranded costs also must be addressed by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission.

"If a former wholesale requirements customer or a former retail customer uses the new open access to reach a new supplier, we believe that the utility is entitled to recover legitimate, prudent and verifiable costs that it incurred under the prior regulatory regime to serve that customer, the commmission ruled.
In the ruling, the commission specifically noted that municipalization of a public utility constitutes such a wholesale-turned-retail situation, El Paso said.

It said the "condemnation effort appears to rest on the untenable assumption that Las Cruces could take our system without having to compensate us for a proportionate share of strandable costs," said chief executive James Haines.

"If even a low estimate of strandable cost responsibility is included in the economic model of Las Cruces' plan, a Las Cruces municipal utility would have to increase rates in order to cover its fixed costs."
El Paso Electric said the customers it serves within the City of Las Cruces contributed seven percent of its operating revenues in 1996.
